title: Synergistic Graphene and PEDOT:PSS Layers on Silicon for Enhanced Efficiency and Stability in Schottky Junction Solar Cells
authors: Kentaro Nakajo, Hojun Im, Keiichiro Nishimura, Masahiro Teraoka, Masaya Kikuchi
abstract: While graphene/n-type silicon (Gr/n-Si) and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si solar cells offer a cost-effective alternative to conventional photovoltaics, achieving simultaneous high power conversion efficiency (PCE) and long-term environmental stability remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report the synergistic enhancement of both performance and stability in a planar trilayer PEDOT:PSS/Gr/n-Si Schottky junction architecture. By systematically benchmarking this hybrid device against pristine Gr/n-Si and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si reference cells fabricated on untextured substrates, we isolate the fundamental optoelectronic and barrier functions of the carbon lattice. Comprehensive analyses reveal that the PEDOT:PSS layer simultaneously functions as an anti-reflection coating, a moderate p-type dopant for the underlying graphene, and a conductivity enhancer, collectively optimizing interfacial charge transport. Consequently, the trilayer device achieves a PCE of 8.52%, markedly outperforming the pristine Gr/n-Si reference cell (4.56%). Crucially, the atomic impermeability of the graphene sheet serves as a robust environmental barrier. While bare PEDOT:PSS/n-Si junctions retained only ~29% of their initial efficiency after 75 days of ambient exposure, graphene shields the active junction from moisture-induced degradation of the hygroscopic PEDOT:PSS overlayer. This enables the trilayer device to retain approximately 90% of its initial efficiency over the same 75-day period. The complementary roles of graphene as both a highly crystalline charge transport interface and an impermeable protective barrier establish a highly effective strategy for engineering high-efficiency, environmentally stable hybrid photovoltaics.

infographic.key_insight: A PEDOT:PSS/graphene/n-Si trilayer combines optical, electrical, and barrier functions to boost both efficiency and environmental stability in Schottky solar cells.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work suggests a practical low-cost interface stack for silicon photovoltaics that improves charge collection while protecting hygroscopic organic layers from ambient degradation.
method: Benchmark trilayer PEDOT:PSS/Gr/n-Si against Gr/n-Si and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si reference cells.
Use PEDOT:PSS as an anti-reflection coating, mild p-type dopant for graphene, and conductivity enhancer.
Leverage graphene as both a charge-transport interface and moisture barrier.
infographic.evidence_signal: The trilayer device reached 8.52% PCE versus 4.56% for Gr/n-Si, and retained about 90% of initial efficiency after 75 days in ambient conditions, compared with ~29% for PEDOT:PSS/n-Si.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and stability gains were shown on untextured substrates, so scaling to textured or large-area manufacturing may change the optical and interfacial balance.
infographic.paper_title: Synergistic Graphene and PEDOT:PSS Layers on Silicon for Enhanced Efficiency and Stability in Schottky Junction Solar Cells

title: High-Throughput Imaging of Degradation-Inducing Microscopic Impurities in Perovskite Solar Cells
authors: Sofiia Kosar, Anil R. Pininti, Vladyslav Hnapovskyi, José P. Jurado, Subhashri Mannar, Lorenzo Mardegan
abstract: The scalable fabrication of high-quality, large-area perovskite thin films is hindered by microscopic inhomogeneities, particularly residual compositional impurities formed during processing. Identifying these impurities, understanding their impact on device operation, and enabling their rapid detection are essential for upscaling perovskite solar cells (PSCs). Here, nano-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy combined with high-resolution optical and scanning probe techniques was used to identify detrimental impurities in wide-bandgap perovskite films relevant to tandem solar cells. Photo-stress experiments revealed that degradation of the perovskite layer initiates at impurity-perovskite interfaces, demonstrating that impurities act as failure nucleation sites. Leveraging these insights, a rapid, non-invasive, and high-throughput framework based on high-resolution reflected light microscopy and machine learning-supported image analysis was developed, enabling detection and quantification of harmful impurities in as-prepared films within seconds. Films with higher impurity density show accelerated early degradation, establishing this parameter as an early-warning metric for stability screening. Extending this framework to degradation tracking further reveals coupled photo- and thermo-chemical contributions to impurity-mediated instability. Overall, this work establishes a practical chemically-validated diagnostic imaging framework for rapid pre-screening of perovskite films to enable stable and scalable PSCs.

infographic.key_insight: Microscopic residual impurities in perovskite films are not just defects—they are degradation hot spots that nucleate failure at impurity–perovskite interfaces.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study provides a fast, non-invasive imaging-and-AI screening workflow to flag unstable perovskite films before device fabrication, supporting scalable quality control for solar cell manufacturing.
method: Nano-FTIR chemically identified harmful residual impurities in wide-bandgap perovskite films.
High-resolution reflected-light microscopy plus machine-learning image analysis enabled rapid impurity detection in seconds.
Photo-stress and thermo-photo degradation tracking linked impurity density to early failure onset.
infographic.evidence_signal: Chemically validated imaging showed that degradation starts at impurity–perovskite interfaces, and films with higher impurity density exhibited accelerated early degradation.
infographic.watch_item: The workflow depends on calibration to chemically validated impurity signatures, so performance may vary across film compositions, processing routes, and imaging setups.
infographic.paper_title: High-Throughput Imaging of Degradation-Inducing Microscopic Impurities in Perovskite Solar Cells

title: Provenance-grouped protocol for evaluating machine learning in perovskite photovoltaics
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou
abstract: Machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells are typically evaluated using random data splits, which we show systematically leak information through massive internal duplication. Because nearly two-thirds of curated devices share their exact recipe with another, random splits primarily reward the mere recall of historical data rather than testing true physical generalisation. To solve this, we mapped the institutional provenance of the Perovskite Database and established a rigorous hierarchy of grouped splits that progressively isolate duplicate devices, publications, and institutions. Benchmarking thirteen models establishes new state-of-the-art performance across all splits and reveals a critical regime shift: while tree ensembles dominate random splits by recognising familiar recipes, their ranking collapses on genuinely unseen institutions and future discoveries, where composition-aware neural architectures excel. Furthermore, feature importance demonstrates that the device architecture and fabrication methodology dictate final efficiency just as strongly as the absorber chemistry. This standardised protocol empowers the community to separate memorisation from true physical discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Random data splits overestimate ML performance for perovskite photovoltaics because duplicate and near-duplicate devices leak across train/test sets; grouped splits expose the difference between memorization and true generalization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A provenance-aware evaluation protocol helps researchers choose and trust models that better predict performance for new institutions, recipes, and future perovskite devices.
method: Mapped institutional provenance in the Perovskite Database
Built a hierarchy of grouped splits that isolate duplicates, publications, and institutions
Benchmarked 13 models across increasingly strict evaluation settings
infographic.evidence_signal: Nearly two-thirds of curated devices share an exact recipe with another, and model rankings change sharply when evaluation moves from random splits to unseen institutions and future discoveries.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on the completeness and accuracy of provenance mapping, so missing or ambiguous metadata could weaken the grouped-split protocol.
infographic.paper_title: Provenance-grouped protocol for evaluating machine learning in perovskite photovoltaics

title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou
abstract: Existing machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells struggle to predict devices made from new materials. Most treat device layers as arbitrary categorical labels and represent perovskite absorbers either through featureless composition vectors or through rigid crystal graphs that require a pre-solved unit cell. As a result, they cannot generalize to unrecorded alloys or unfamiliar cell architectures. We present the Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System (V-PaSS), an architecture built around the physical continuity of perovskite solid solutions. V-PaSS represents arbitrary mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers by interpolating relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure $ABX_3$ endpoint compounds via Vegard's law with learned bandgap bowing. For the device stack, it couples layer sequence and cell polarity (n-i-p or p-i-n) with interfacial band offsets and encodes chemical descriptions with a scientific language model. Evaluated under an institution-grouped protocol where test devices come exclusively from unseen laboratories, an untuned default configuration of V-PaSS achieves the lowest error among fourteen tested models (2.861% MAE, a 5.2% relative reduction over a gradient-boosted baseline at 3.017%, and outperforming the best tuned benchmark at 2.912%). V-PaSS pulls furthest ahead where test devices differ most from training: reducing error by 15.7-19.0% on unseen absorber alloys, by 16.1% on mixed absorbers from new laboratories, and widening its lead over the baseline by 3.6$\times$ on devices with unobserved transport layers. Combined with tree ensembles, V-PaSS sets a new state of the art across all five benchmark splits.

infographic.key_insight: V-PaSS improves perovskite solar-cell prediction by modeling absorber alloys and device stacks with physics-aware representations instead of treating them as simple categories.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more reliable extrapolation to new perovskite compositions, unfamiliar layer stacks, and unseen laboratories, which is crucial for accelerating device design and screening.
method: Interpolates mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers from 23 relaxed pure ABX3 crystal-graph endpoints using Vegard’s law plus learned bandgap bowing.
Encodes device architecture with layer sequence, polarity, interfacial band offsets, and scientific-language-model embeddings for chemistry text.
Evaluates under an institution-grouped split to test generalization to completely unseen labs and materials.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under the unseen-laboratory evaluation, V-PaSS achieved 2.861% MAE, outperforming strong baselines and showing the largest gains on unseen alloys and transport layers.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on reliable endpoint crystal structures and learned bowing parameters, so performance may degrade when those physical inputs are sparse or poorly characterized.
infographic.paper_title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells

title: PING: physics informed graph neural network for advection-diffusion processes with applications to solar power forecasting
authors: Jelena Simeunović, Baptiste Schubnel, Pierre-Jean Alet, Pascal Frossard, Rafael E. Carrillo
abstract: Advection-diffusion plays an essential role in transport phenomena such as atmospheric and cloud dynamics. Improved forecasting of cloud motion, in turn, enhances solar power production forecasts and facilitates the integration of additional photovoltaic (PV) sources into the power grid. However, both classical numerical models and emerging deep learning approaches face challenges when applied to spatially irregular sensor networks such as those formed by weather stations. In this work, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective and model advection-diffusion particles as signals on a graph to capture the dynamics of these processes. We introduce a Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PING) for forecasting future advection-diffusion particle concentrations on irregular grids. The model incorporates a discretized advection-diffusion equation as a soft constraint in the loss function to guide learning toward physically consistent solutions. This model is on par with state of the art models on synthetic and real transport phenomena datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index datasets. Furthermore, the PING model is successfully coupled with models for forecasting PV power production. This hybrid approach leverages data fusion from ground-based sensors at PV stations and satellite images with cloud concentration to improve the accuracy of intra-day PV power production.

infographic.key_insight: PING uses a physics-informed graph neural network to forecast advection-diffusion on irregular sensor networks, improving cloud-motion prediction for solar power forecasting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can strengthen intra-day PV production forecasts by fusing ground sensors and satellite-derived cloud information, helping grid operators integrate more solar generation reliably.
method: Model advection-diffusion particles as graph signals on irregular grids.
Embed a discretized advection-diffusion equation as a soft loss constraint.
Combine the forecast with PV models using ground-based sensor and satellite cloud data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports performance on synthetic and real transport datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index data, and says the model is on par with state-of-the-art methods.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of irregular sensor coverage and the fidelity of the discretized physics prior, which may limit robustness under sparse or noisy observations.
infographic.paper_title: PING: physics informed graph neural network for advection-diffusion processes with applications to solar power forecasting

title: Device Model Linking Singlet and Triplet Spin-State Properties to Organic Photovoltaic Device Characteristics
authors: Jun Du, Liming Liu, Jun Yan
abstract: This work proposes an exciton-kinetics coupled drift-diffusion (EKDD) model that bridges device-level charge transport with singlet and triplet excited-state kinetics. State populations and reversible photophysical transitions are solved self-consistently, enabling transient and steady-state device response calculations. We investigate how LE-CT, CT-CS, and LE-T energy offsets, together with triplet-transfer kinetics, govern charge generation, recombination, voltage loss, and extraction in organic photovoltaics. We identify CT-CS offset as a primary, largely overlooked factor controlling charge generation and voltage loss. A positive offset makes CT3-CS separation exothermic and improves generation, but lowers CS energy and increases voltage loss; a negative offset makes separation endothermic and highly temperature-sensitive. The model reproduces triplet-mediated recombination in PM6:Y6 and material-dependent triplet recycling in D18:NFA blends. We propose design rules for balanced generation and voltage loss via two charge-transfer channels: the LE-CT-CS pathway favors a moderate LE-CT offset of about 0.15-0.20 eV and a weakly exothermic CT-CS offset of about 0.05-0.075 eV; the T-CT3-CS pathway requires the same CT-CS alignment plus a small CT-T offset, no more than about 0.1 eV, corresponding to a recycling factor K greater than about 10^-2, to maintain fast T-to-CT3 recycling. CT-CS alignment is the main determinant of the charge-generation-voltage-loss trade-off, while triplet-recycling kinetics determines whether this balance survives at the device level. This work provides a unified theoretical description from exciton generation to free charge collection, offering a convenient tool for transient and steady-state analysis in organic photovoltaics.

infographic.key_insight: An exciton-kinetics coupled drift-diffusion model shows that CT-CS energy alignment is the main knob controlling the trade-off between charge generation and voltage loss in organic photovoltaics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model gives device designers practical rules for tuning singlet/triplet energetics and triplet recycling to improve photocurrent while limiting voltage penalties.
method: Self-consistent exciton-kinetics coupled drift-diffusion simulation of charge transport and excited-state populations
Includes reversible singlet/triplet transitions with LE-CT, CT-CS, and LE-T offsets
Analyzes transient and steady-state behavior to separate generation, recombination, extraction, and voltage-loss effects
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the model reproduces triplet-mediated recombination in PM6:Y6 and material-dependent triplet recycling in D18:NFA blends.
infographic.watch_item: The recommended CT-CS and CT-T alignments may be highly sensitive to temperature and material-specific energetics, so experimental calibration is needed before transfer to new blends.
infographic.paper_title: Device Model Linking Singlet and Triplet Spin-State Properties to Organic Photovoltaic Device Characteristics

title: Engineering Color and Angular Stability in Building-Integrated Photovoltaics Using Metal-Oxide Photonic Glasses
authors: Sinan Genc, Talat Ozden, Alpan Bek
abstract: Coloring building-integrated photovoltaics poses a dilemma: absorptive pigments cost photocurrent, while ordered photonic structures are iridescent. Amorphous photonic glasses, disordered packings of high-index nanospheres, are proposed to avoid both, yet their angle-independent color has rarely been quantified on a realistic module stack. A non-absorbing scatterer needs a high index with visible transparency, which the Moss rule caps near 2.35. Coupling Mie scattering, the Percus-Yevick structure factor, the exact phase function, and two-flux transfer with absorption and refraction at the front glass, we fix four target colors that a crowd-sourced naming survey calls unambiguously blue, green, gold, and terracotta, and map the recipes reaching them across four metal oxides, four encapsulants, two cell technologies, and wide ranges of particle size, packing fraction, and layer number. All four are reached in a laminated three-layer coating, to within DeltaE00 of 0.8 to 2.5, but not from one oxide: transparent TiO2 renders the blue and only pale warm tones; the green, gold, and terracotta require the blue-band absorption of V2O5, and the low-contrast oxides turn grey at the warm end. The encapsulant governs the color, and the cell technology does not. Disorder does not confer angle independence: the colors hold for an observer moving under a fixed sun but drift by DeltaE00 of 5 to 18 over the day, terracotta least, and a facade lit from above and viewed from below shifts every color towards the blue. Oxide, layer number, and facade geometry must therefore be designed together.

infographic.key_insight: Disordered metal-oxide photonic glasses can produce building-integrated PV colors without strong iridescence, but the achievable color depends more on oxide choice and stack design than on disorder alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work provides a practical design map for tunable, low-loss colored PV facades, helping engineers balance aesthetics, spectral selectivity, and power yield.
method: Modeled color formation using Mie scattering, Percus–Yevick structure factors, exact phase functions, and two-flux transfer.
Explored four target facade colors across four oxides, four encapsulants, two cell technologies, and wide ranges of particle size, packing fraction, and layer count.
Evaluated color shift under realistic viewing and sun-angle changes on a laminated three-layer coating stack.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that all four target colors were reached within DeltaE00 0.8 to 2.5 in a laminated three-layer coating, while angular variation caused DeltaE00 shifts of 5 to 18 over the day.
infographic.watch_item: Angle independence is limited in realistic use: facade geometry and sun/view angles can noticeably shift perceived color, so the coating must be co-designed with installation conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Engineering Color and Angular Stability in Building-Integrated Photovoltaics Using Metal-Oxide Photonic Glasses

title: Engineering Correlated Transparent Conductors via Metal-Insulator Transition Proximity
authors: Amit Cohen, Nofar Tuval, Maria Baskin, Tien-Lin Lee, Tom Tiwald, Scott A. Chambers
abstract: Transparent conductors are key functional materials in modern optoelectronic devices. Their performance is governed by an inherent trade-off between optical transparency and electrical conductivity. Correlated metallic oxides offer an attractive workaround to this compromise, where narrow partially-filled bands provide high conductivity, while the absence of visible-range transitions enables optical transparency. Despite this promise, transparency and conductivity remain coupled through carrier density and electronic coherence. Here, we use proximity to a metal-insulator transition (MIT) as a design principle for engineering this balance in correlated-oxide transparent conductors. Epitaxial Ti-substituted $SrVO_3$ films serve as a model platform where the optical window and metallicity are tuned simultaneously. We demonstrate and explain a systematic broadening of the optical window to regimes relevant for silicon photovoltaics. This gain is counterbalanced by carrier depletion and disorder, which drive the loss of coherent transport near the composition-driven MIT. A Haacke figure-of-merit analysis identifies the optimal composition range near the MIT, where the loss of metallic transport is accompanied by persistent near-Fermi-level spectral weight, indicating disorder-assisted localization together with correlation-driven spectral-weight redistribution. These findings establish proximity to an MIT as a general materials-design strategy, using electronic filling as a tuning knob for the transparency-conductivity balance in correlated-oxide transparent conductors.

infographic.key_insight: Proximity to a metal-insulator transition can be used to tune correlated-oxide transparent conductors so they gain a wider optical window while retaining useful near-Fermi-level states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical materials-design rule for optimizing transparent electrodes for silicon photovoltaics and other optoelectronic devices by balancing transparency against conductivity.
method: Used epitaxial Ti-substituted SrVO3 films as a tunable model system.
Varied composition to approach the metal-insulator transition and simultaneously track optical and transport properties.
Analyzed performance with a Haacke figure of merit to identify the best composition range.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a systematic broadening of the optical window toward silicon-relevant wavelengths, with the best figure-of-merit occurring near the composition-driven metal-insulator transition.
infographic.watch_item: Near the optimal transparency range, carrier depletion and disorder reduce coherent transport, so the approach may be limited by the loss of metallic conductivity and sensitivity to disorder.
infographic.paper_title: Engineering Correlated Transparent Conductors via Metal-Insulator Transition Proximity

title: Dual-Resonator Organic Microcavities for Triplet-Triplet Annihilation Upconversion
authors: Robert H. Gordon, Rachel C. Kilbride, Michael Hutton, Jenny Clark, Robert D. J. Oliver
abstract: Solid-state triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion offers a compelling route to harvest sub-bandgap photons to increase the efficiency of photovoltaics, but low sensitizer doping required to suppress non-radiative aggregation quenching severely restricts light absorption. Here, we present a dual-resonator planar silver microcavity housing a thermally co-evaporated rubrene:palladium phthalocyanine (PdPC) active layer designed to simultaneously enhance triplet-sensitizer absorption and out-couple upconverted emission. By aligning a dispersive cavity mode with the PdPC absorption peak at $32^\circ$, we achieve a 12-fold enhancement in absorptance at 665 nm. This absorption boost, combined with directional outcoupling through a second cavity mode, outweighs cavity-induced reabsorption losses to yield a 22-fold peak and 4.5-fold integrated enhancement in detected upconversion emission. Overall, this work highlights the potential of microcavity integration to substantially enhance solid-state upconversion performance across low-intensity optoelectronic applications.

infographic.key_insight: A dual-resonator silver microcavity can simultaneously boost triplet sensitizer absorption and direct upconverted emission, overcoming the usual tradeoff in solid-state triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach could make low-intensity sub-bandgap photon harvesting more practical for photovoltaic and other optoelectronic devices by increasing usable emission without requiring higher sensitizer loading.
method: Thermally co-evaporated a rubrene:palladium phthalocyanine active layer inside a planar silver microcavity.
Aligned one dispersive cavity mode with the PdPC absorption peak at 32° to enhance sensitizer absorption.
Used a second cavity mode to directionally out-couple upconverted emission while managing reabsorption losses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a 12-fold absorptance increase at 665 nm, a 22-fold peak increase in detected upconversion emission, and a 4.5-fold enhancement when integrated over emission.
infographic.watch_item: Microcavity benefits may depend on precise angle/mode alignment, and reabsorption plus aggregation-quenching constraints still limit practical device optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Dual-Resonator Organic Microcavities for Triplet-Triplet Annihilation Upconversion

title: Material chemical composition impacts on the band alignments: preliminary results on the 3D/2D perovskite interfaces
authors: Philippe Baranek
abstract: While hybrid organic-inorganic halide perovskite solar cells have achieved remarkable certified efficiencies, their widespread industrial and societal adoption is hindered by instabilities against light, heat, and moisture. A strategy to mitigate issues, such as moisture sensitivity, involves depositing 2D perovskites on 3D thin films for passivation, but their precise impact on cell performance requires detailed understanding. This work employs atomistic first-principles simulation, based on hybrid functionals, to investigate the structural and electronic properties of 2D/3D interfaces. Specifically, it focuses on interfaces formed by (PEA)2PbI4 (PEA = C6H5CH2CH2NH3, as 2D perovskite) and complex 3D perovskites (Cs0.125MA0.14FA0.735Pb(I0.87Br0.13)3, with MA = CH3NH3 and FA = CH(NH2)2) which are ones of the most used perovskites. The approach is based on optimized hybrid functional methods to consistently determine work function (WF), electron affinity, and band offset (EBO) across different layers. Preliminary results demonstrate that WF are strongly dependent on the cleavage and chemical nature of the surfaces. Furthermore, the creation of interfaces significantly impacts macroscopic potential, with a noticeable slope linked to the polarization of the 3D materials due to ionic substitutions. The band alignment is also highly sensitive to the termination and chemical nature of the perovskites, with valence and conduction EBOs varying from 0.2 to 0.7 eV and of approximately 0.25 eV, respectively. This ongoing work aims to provide a systematic description of these effects, with further investigation into the impact of dimensionality loss on perovskite stability.

infographic.key_insight: The 2D/3D perovskite band alignment is highly sensitive to surface termination and chemical composition, with interface-induced polarization strongly shifting the local electrostatic landscape.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results help guide interface engineering in perovskite solar cells by showing how passivating 2D layers can alter work function and band offsets, affecting charge extraction and stability.
method: Atomistic first-principles simulations using hybrid functionals
Modeled (PEA)2PbI4 / 3D perovskite interfaces with different terminations and compositions
Computed work function, electron affinity, and band offsets across layers
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports preliminary calculated shifts in valence band offsets of about 0.2 to 0.7 eV and conduction offsets of about 0.25 eV, depending on termination and chemistry.
infographic.watch_item: Results are preliminary and depend on specific surface cleavages and modeled compositions, so broader device-level performance implications still need validation.
infographic.paper_title: Material chemical composition impacts on the band alignments: preliminary results on the 3D/2D perovskite interfaces

title: Tellurium trioxide as an n-type wide-gap semiconductor with ultrahigh work functions from first principles
authors: Tianwei Wang, Teruya Nagafuji, Kota Hanzawa, Hidenori Hiramatsu, Fumiyasu Oba
abstract: The exploration of next-generation wide-gap semiconductors with extreme work functions is highly desirable for the continued advancement of electronic and optoelectronic devices. By using first principles calculations, we show that \b{eta}-TeO3, with a wide band gap exceeding 3 eV, emerges as a promising n-type semiconductor exhibiting ultrahigh work functions of up to ~8 eV. Intentionally or unintentionally incorporated interstitial H, Li, Na, Cu, Mg, and Zn impurities and substitutional F impurities are identified as shallow donors, whereas O vacancies act as minor carrier-compensating defects that locally trap electrons at neighbouring Te sites. The work function is evaluated across a series of low-index nonpolar surfaces. The presence of ordered O vacancies is energetically favoured on these surfaces and tends to reduce the corresponding work functions. These findings underscore the significance of precise control over the O chemical potential to suppress surface O-vacancy formation, thereby preserving the exceptional electronic performance of \b{eta}-TeO3 associated with ultrahigh work functions. Collectively, the results highlight the potential of \b{eta}-TeO3 for hole injection/extraction/transport layers as well as transparent electrodes for applications such as light-emitting devices and photovoltaic cells, while providing useful guidance on carrier doping and surface tuning for these practical applications through elucidating the effects of the point-defect and surface configurations on the electronic properties.

infographic.key_insight: β-TeO3 is predicted to be a wide-band-gap n-type semiconductor with exceptionally high work functions, reaching about 8 eV, making it promising for charge-injection and transparent-electrode roles.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its defect and surface chemistry suggest it could serve in photovoltaic and light-emitting device stacks, but performance depends strongly on controlling oxygen vacancies and chemical potential during growth.
method: First-principles calculations of the electronic structure and defect energetics.
Assessment of point defects including H, Li, Na, Cu, Mg, Zn, F, and oxygen vacancies.
Work-function evaluation across low-index nonpolar surfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a band gap above 3 eV, shallow-donor behavior for several impurities, and surface-dependent work functions up to ~8 eV, with oxygen vacancies lowering the work function.
infographic.watch_item: Surface oxygen-vacancy formation can reduce the ultrahigh work function, so growth and post-processing must tightly control oxygen chemical potential.
infographic.paper_title: Tellurium trioxide as an n-type wide-gap semiconductor with ultrahigh work functions from first principles

title: Wavelength-Dependent Photoluminescence Mapping of Depth-Dependent Degradation Under Thermal Stress in Phenethylammonium Tetrafluoroborate Treated Perovskite Solar Cells
authors: Julisa Juarez, Akash Dasgupta, Alan Zhan, Lamtiur P. Samosir, David S. Ginger*
abstract: Studying real-time degradation in perovskite semiconductors remains an important challenge. Conventional methods often cannot separate interfacial and bulk processes or rely on destructive analysis. Here, we demonstrate multiwavelength excitation photoluminescence (PL) as a nondestructive approach to distinguish interface- and bulk-dominated recombination losses. Using phenethylammonium tetrafluoroborate (PEABF4) treatment as a model, we use PL to show that PEABF4 passivates the electron transport layer (ETL)/perovskite interface, reducing interfacial recombination losses from fullerene deposition. However, upon thermal aging, PEABF4-treated stacks degrade more rapidly, with recombination losses broadening from the ETL/perovskite interface into the absorber. Diffusion-recombination simulations support interpreting excitation-wavelength-dependent PL decay signatures consistent with changes in surface recombination velocity and bulk lifetime, providing a framework for depth-sensitive comparisons during aging. Collectively, these results further establish multiwavelength excitation PL as a platform for studying recombination losses during aging of perovskite films.

infographic.key_insight: Multiwavelength excitation photoluminescence can non-destructively distinguish whether recombination losses in perovskite solar cells originate near the ETL/perovskite interface or deeper in the absorber, and it reveals that PEABF4 passivation slows initial interfacial loss but accelerates broader thermal degradation over time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a depth-sensitive diagnostic for evaluating interface treatments and aging mechanisms in perovskite solar cells, helping engineers target stability improvements without destructive sectioning.
method: Used wavelength-dependent PL excitation to probe different carrier generation depths.
Compared untreated and PEABF4-treated perovskite stacks during thermal aging.
Interpreted PL decay trends with diffusion-recombination simulations to separate surface recombination velocity from bulk lifetime changes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that PEABF4 reduces interfacial recombination from fullerene deposition initially, but under thermal stress the PL decay signatures broaden from the ETL/perovskite interface into the absorber, consistent with worsening bulk and interfacial losses.
infographic.watch_item: PL-based depth interpretation is model-dependent, so excitation-depth assumptions and simulation parameters must be carefully validated for each stack architecture.
infographic.paper_title: Wavelength-Dependent Photoluminescence Mapping of Depth-Dependent Degradation Under Thermal Stress in Phenethylammonium Tetrafluoroborate Treated Perovskite Solar Cells

title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites
authors: Simone Grillo, Offir Zachs Maishlos, Liya Koren, Rotem Strassberg, Rachel Lifer, Edi Maizenberg
abstract: Double perovskites (DPs) offer a compositionally versatile platform for photocatalysis and optoelectronics, but their soft lattices favor strong exciton-phonon coupling and self-trapped excitons (STEs), which produce broad, red-shifted photoluminescence (PL). Here, we combine optical spectroscopy and ab initio calculations to study lead-free, Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals with B-site alloying from Na to K. Alloying tunes the PL energy from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV, while absorption features near 3.8 eV remain nearly unchanged. Calculations reveal that Sb doping enables bright radiative recombination channels and delocalizes the excitonic wavefunction. We identify STEs responsible for the large PL red shift, associated with an upward shift of dopant-hybridized in-gap states. Na-to-K substitution selectively changes the STE lattice distortion, explaining why PL varies strongly with composition while absorption does not. Theory further predicts pronounced PL polarization anisotropy that reflects the STE wavefunction's spatial structure and depends on B-site composition. Time-resolved anisotropy measurements closely agree with these predictions, providing experimental fingerprints of the excitonic wavefunction and its evolution with alloying. Together, these results disentangle the roles of doping and alloying in lead-free DPs and establish polarization-resolved spectroscopy as a probe of STE wavefunctions.

infographic.key_insight: Sb doping in Cs2BInCl6 double perovskite nanocrystals creates self-trapped excitons whose emission energy and polarization fingerprints can be tuned by Na-to-K alloying.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a composition-guided route to engineer lead-free perovskite emitters with controllable color and anisotropic photoluminescence for optoelectronic and photocatalytic devices.
method: Optical spectroscopy on Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals with B-site alloying from Na to K
Ab initio calculations of excitonic states and lattice distortions
Time-resolved polarization anisotropy measurements to probe STE wavefunction structure
infographic.evidence_signal: PL shifts from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV while absorption near 3.8 eV stays nearly unchanged, and measured anisotropy closely matches theory.
infographic.watch_item: The strong PL behavior depends on soft-lattice self-trapping, so device stability and reproducibility may be sensitive to composition and structural disorder.
infographic.paper_title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites

title: Disorder-Induced Griffiths like Phase and Charge Localization in Sr2FeRuO6
authors: Koustav Pal, Shuvendu Ghosh, I. Das
abstract: A comprehensive understanding of complex transition-metal oxides is key to designing next-generation spintronic materials with tailored magnetic and transport functionalities. We investigate the interplay among structural disorder, frustrated magnetism, and localized charge transport in the 3d-4d hybrid double perovskite Sr2FeRuO6. The compound adopts a monoclinic structure with significant B-site antisite disorder that drives its unconventional behavior. Magnetic measurements uncover a robust Griffiths phase extending well above the ordering temperature, evidencing stable short-range ferromagnetic clusters within a disordered matrix. Electrical transport remains strongly localized, transitioning from small-polaron hopping at high temperatures to variable-range hopping at intermediate temperatures. These results position Sr2FeRuO6 as a representative 3d-4d hybrid system in which quenched disorder stabilizes spin inhomogeneity, while polaronic and hopping transport are also observed.

infographic.key_insight: Although this paper is about a disordered double perovskite rather than a solar cell, its central finding is that B-site antisite disorder in Sr2FeRuO6 stabilizes Griffiths-like magnetic clusters and strongly localized charge transport.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results highlight how structural disorder and cation mixing can profoundly alter magnetic and transport behavior in oxide materials, informing defect-aware design of functional perovskites for spintronic and electronic applications.
method: Monoclinic structure analysis of Sr2FeRuO6 with significant B-site antisite disorder
Magnetic measurements to identify a Griffiths phase and short-range ferromagnetic clusters
Electrical transport analysis comparing small-polaron hopping and variable-range hopping regimes
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports robust Griffiths-phase behavior above the magnetic ordering temperature and a clear temperature-dependent transport crossover from small-polaron hopping to variable-range hopping.
infographic.watch_item: Because the conclusions rely on disordered bulk oxide behavior, performance and reproducibility may be highly sensitive to sample stoichiometry, antisite disorder level, and synthesis conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Disorder-Induced Griffiths like Phase and Charge Localization in Sr2FeRuO6

title: Effect of deep-trap density of states for a-Si:H layers on HIT cell performances: Modeling Framework
authors: Tewfik Souier, Adel Gougam
abstract: In this work, an aSi and cSi heterojunction solar cell with an intrinsic layer is simulated using AFORS-HET software. The study focuses on the role of the electronic density of states DOS of the amorphous emitter, p type aSiH, in governing the performance of the HIT cell and the electronic transfer across the heterointerface. It is found that the DOS of the p type aSiH emitter can cause an unfavorable recombination and trapping effect, which becomes more severe and difficult to avoid when the bulk dangling-bond density in the a-Si emitter approaches or exceeds the doping concentration. An increase in deep trap density beyond a critical value causes a drop in the built in voltage and shifts the depletion layer into p type aSi. This situation leads to a sharp decline in HIT cell performance, namely the open circuit voltage and the fill factor, and to the appearance of an S shaped IV characteristic. The simulation results suggest that the emitter activation energy needs to be optimized to achieve high efficiency. Under optimal conditions, holes accumulate near the heterojunction interface, leading to the formation of an inversion layer. This paper presents a physical mechanism for recombination processes within the emitter and concludes with the optimized parameters required to achieve a HIT cell efficiency comparable to Sanyo record of 23 percent on a thin silicon wafer.

infographic.key_insight: Increasing deep-trap density in the p-type a-Si:H emitter degrades HIT cell performance by enhancing recombination, lowering built-in voltage, and can trigger S-shaped I-V behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing the emitter activation energy and deep-level defect density is critical to preserve Voc and fill factor in high-efficiency a-Si:H/c-Si heterojunction solar cells.
method: Simulated a-Si:H/c-Si HIT solar cells with AFORS-HET.
Varied the electronic density of states of the p-type a-Si:H emitter, especially deep dangling-bond traps.
Evaluated how defect density affects band bending, depletion region position, and I-V performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that once deep-trap density exceeds a critical value, Voc and fill factor drop sharply and an S-shaped I-V curve appears, consistent with strong recombination losses.
infographic.watch_item: The optimized performance depends sensitively on realistic emitter defect and activation-energy values, so fabrication variability could make the predicted optimum hard to reproduce.
infographic.paper_title: Effect of deep-trap density of states for a-Si:H layers on HIT cell performances: Modeling Framework

title: Theoretical Investigation of Oxygen-Vacancy Diffusion in SrTiO$_3$ using Neural Network Potentials
authors: Kazutaka Nishiguchi, Ryota Yamamoto, Seiichiro Ten-no
abstract: Oxygen-vacancy formation and diffusion play important roles in determining the electronic and atomic transport properties of SrTiO$_3$ (STO). Accurate analysis of such point defects requires sufficiently large-scale and long-time molecular dynamics (MD) simulations; however, direct investigations of oxygen-vacancy dynamics using {\it ab initio} MD (AIMD) based on density functional theory (DFT) are limited to relatively small systems and short time scales because of their high computational cost. In this study, we develop a neural network potential (NNP) for pristine and oxygen-deficient STO using a reference dataset generated from AIMD simulations. The trained NNP model accurately reproduces the DFT reference energies, atomic forces, and virials for both pristine STO and STO containing an oxygen vacancy. The NNP also reproduces the supercell-size dependence of the total energies and oxygen-vacancy formation energies, including the formation energy extrapolated to the dilute limit. Large-scale and long-time MD simulations using the NNP (NNP-MD) are then performed to investigate oxygen-vacancy diffusion. The resulting oxygen-vacancy diffusion coefficients show substantially better agreement with experimental data than those obtained from conventional classical MD simulations. An Arrhenius analysis yields an oxygen-vacancy migration enthalpy of 0.64 eV, in close agreement with the experimental value of 0.67 eV. These results demonstrate that NNPs trained on first-principles data provide an accurate and computationally efficient framework for investigating defect formation and long-time vacancy transport in perovskite oxides.

infographic.key_insight: A neural network potential trained on DFT data can accurately model oxygen-vacancy formation and long-time diffusion in SrTiO3 at scales impractical for ab initio MD.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables reliable, large-scale defect-transport simulations for perovskite oxides, improving prediction of degradation, conductivity, and device-relevant defect behavior.
method: Generated a DFT/AIMD reference dataset for pristine and oxygen-deficient SrTiO3.
Trained a neural network potential to reproduce energies, forces, virials, and vacancy formation energies.
Ran large-scale NNP-MD and extracted oxygen-vacancy diffusion coefficients and Arrhenius migration enthalpy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The NNP matches DFT reference properties and yields a 0.64 eV migration enthalpy, close to the experimental 0.67 eV.
infographic.watch_item: The model is validated for SrTiO3 defect chemistry, but transferability to other compositions, defect types, or strongly different thermodynamic conditions may require retraining.
infographic.paper_title: Theoretical Investigation of Oxygen-Vacancy Diffusion in SrTiO$_3$ using Neural Network Potentials

title: Dynamic Chemical Changes of Ti3C2Tx MXenes in Halide Perovskite Precursor Environments
authors: Kirill Sobolev, Nagaprasad Reddy Samala, Mariela J. Pavan, Sharon Hazan, Vladimir Ezersky, Shakked Schwartz
abstract: The integration of two-dimensional Ti3C2Tx MXenes into Halide Perovskite (HaP) optoelectronics has shown immense potential for enhancing device performance, yet the fundamental chemical interactions within the precursor ink (a critical stage determining the final material state) remain largely unexplored. This study presents a comprehensive investigation into the chemical stability and surface evolution of Ti3C2Tx MXenes when exposed to the individual and combined components of a model methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) solution. By combining detailed X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) analysis with Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations, we decouple the complex interactions between MXenes and the ink constituents. We demonstrate that elemental iodine (I2) and polyiodides (In-) act as aggressive oxidizers, triggering rapid degradation and dissolution of the MXene flakes. Conversely, lead iodide (PbI2) induces a slower oxidation process driven by the strong adsorption of Pb2+ ions onto oxygen terminated sites. In stark contrast, methylammonium iodide (MAI) exhibits a stabilizing effect: it adsorbs onto the MXene surface via hydrogen bonding, effectively passivating the flakes and retarding degradation. In addition, our results reveal that the sequence of precursor addition governs the MXene surface state, requiring extra caution, but also enabling further tunability. These findings provide a critical view on how MXene integration with materials, in general, and HaP in particular, should be perceived, providing a fundamental for their rational engineering.

infographic.key_insight: Ti3C2Tx MXenes are chemically unstable in halide perovskite precursor inks, but the extent and direction of surface change depend strongly on which precursor species they encounter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: MXene-based perovskite devices must control ink composition and mixing order because iodine species can destroy flakes, while MAI can passivate and help preserve their surface.
method: XPS tracked MXene surface chemistry after exposure to individual and combined MAPbI3 precursor components.
DFT identified adsorption and oxidation pathways for I2, polyiodides, Pb2+, and MAI on Ti3C2Tx surfaces.
Comparative analysis separated aggressive oxidizers from stabilizing adsorbates and linked effects to precursor sequence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a combined XPS and DFT study showing rapid MXene degradation with I2/polyiodides, slower oxidation with PbI2, and stabilization with MAI, including sequence-dependent surface evolution.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on a model MAPbI3 precursor system, so behavior may vary with different perovskite chemistries, solvent conditions, or processing sequences.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamic Chemical Changes of Ti3C2Tx MXenes in Halide Perovskite Precursor Environments

title: Perspective: The HSE Screened Hybrid and the Band Gap Problem: Origins, Impact, and the Contenders
authors: Gustavo E. Scuseria
abstract: The ideas behind the screened hybrid functional HSE took shape in the early 2000s, about a quarter century ago. HSE was not explicitly designed to predict band gaps, although at the time we did recognize that hybrids could help address the band-gap problem. It was designed to make exact exchange affordable and physically defensible in extended systems. Keeping exact exchange at short range and screening it away at long range inverted the prescription developed for molecules. When HSE band gaps for ordinary semiconductors and selected metal oxides came out substantially closer to experiment than those obtained with conventional semilocal approximations, we were pleasantly surprised and encouraged by the path we had taken. The revision from HSE03 to HSE06 improved molecular thermochemistry while preserving the good accuracy for semiconductor gaps. The one-quarter exchange fraction was inherited unchanged from the successful unscreened PBE hybrid for molecules, rather than fitted to solids. HSE established a practical screened-hybrid approach for accurate band-gap calculations, expanding first-principles work in defect physics, photovoltaics, power electronics, and quantum information, among other areas. The first part of this Perspective recounts the decisions made at HSE's birth and their influence on subsequent developments. The second part assesses recent advances in semilocal and hybrid functionals against benchmarks on sets of solids. Recent meta-GGAs achieve HSE06-level accuracy for selected semiconductors, while dielectric-dependent and tuned hybrids address the limitations of fixed screening. These hybrid developments share with our early work on local hybrids and local range separation the aim of adapting exact exchange to the electronic environment. The comparisons assess band gaps alongside structures, energetics, computational cost, and transferability.

infographic.key_insight: HSE made screened exact exchange practical for solids, and that design choice unexpectedly delivered much better band gaps for many semiconductors and oxides than semilocal DFT.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The screened-hybrid framework became a widely used first-principles tool for defect physics, photovoltaics, power electronics, and other materials design problems where accurate electronic gaps matter.
method: Keep exact exchange at short range and screen it at long range to make hybrids affordable in extended systems.
Use the HSE06 revision, which preserved the band-gap performance of HSE while improving molecular thermochemistry.
Benchmark newer semilocal, meta-GGA, dielectric-dependent, and tuned-hybrid functionals against solid-state reference sets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that HSE band gaps for ordinary semiconductors and selected metal oxides were substantially closer to experiment than semilocal approximations, and that recent meta-GGAs can reach HSE06-level accuracy for selected semiconductors.
infographic.watch_item: Fixed screening and a fixed 25% exact-exchange fraction are not universally transferable, so transferability across diverse solids can be limited.
infographic.paper_title: Perspective: The HSE Screened Hybrid and the Band Gap Problem: Origins, Impact, and the Contenders

title: Polarons in Lead-Halide Perovskites: What the Structural Evidence Does and Does Not Establish
authors: Inhee Maeng, Young Mi Lee, Jinwoo Park, Seung Jae Oh, Min-Cherl Jung
abstract: Photogenerated carriers in lead-halide perovskites are widely believed to move as large polarons, whose accompanying lattice distortion is thought to screen the carrier from charged defects. Three recent findings call this picture into question. First, time-resolved structural probes now measure the photoinduced lattice distortion directly; yet calculations show that thermal motion of the lattice alone can raise the carrier effective mass-an increase previously taken as evidence for polarons-so that it remains unclear whether the lattice distortion around a carrier is really a polaron. Second, the carrier-lattice coupling strengthens as the material is thinned from 3D to 2D. In the two main families of 2D perovskites, Ruddlesden-Popper and Dion-Jacobson, the carrier couples to the lattice through different channels, and their contrasting behavior is set by which coupling channel dominates rather than by lattice stiffness alone. Third, the first direct test of defect tolerance does not point to polaron screening; its authors attribute defect tolerance to the soft, disordered lattice. New transport data show that polaron screening reduces scattering between carriers, but not that it protects carriers from defects. Polaron formation, even if established, therefore does not establish polarons as the cause of defect tolerance. Separating the two requires measuring the lattice distortion as a function of excitation density, over a range spanning the low densities of a solar cell under sunlight and the much higher densities used in most ultrafast experiments. On this basis, we propose experiments that can clarify how photogenerated carriers behave in lead-halide perovskites.

infographic.key_insight: Direct structural evidence does not yet prove that photoexcited carriers in lead-halide perovskites form polarons, and polaron formation should not be conflated with defect tolerance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate device design for perovskite solar cells depends on distinguishing carrier-lattice coupling from true defect-screening mechanisms, especially across realistic sunlight-level carrier densities.
method: Compare time-resolved lattice distortion measurements with theory across excitation densities.
Contrast carrier-lattice coupling mechanisms in 3D vs 2D perovskites (Ruddlesden-Popper and Dion-Jacobson).
Test defect tolerance separately from polaron screening using transport and structural probes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract cites recent structural measurements, effective-mass calculations, and new transport data, but notes that these results do not directly establish polaron screening of defects.
infographic.watch_item: Ultrafast experiments often use much higher carrier densities than operating solar cells, so conclusions may not transfer to real device conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Polarons in Lead-Halide Perovskites: What the Structural Evidence Does and Does Not Establish

title: High-throughput computational discovery of CuI-based ternary $p$-type transparent conductors
authors: Michael Seifert, Miguel A. L. Marques, Silvana Botti
abstract: P-type transparent conducting materials (TCMs) remain scarce, limiting progress in transparent electronics and tandem photovoltaics. Here, we perform a high-throughput computational search across CuI-based ternary X--Cu--I compounds using the minima hopping method combined with density functional theory. Filtering for thermodynamic stability, optical transparency, and light hole effective mass, we identify 58 candidate p-type TCMs, of which 49 are previously unreported. Twenty are p-type degenerate semiconductors with intrinsic hole carriers, including Cu$_2$FI$_2$ (calculated gap 3.75 eV, hole effective mass $0.262\,m_0$). We further use this dataset to revisit the chemical modulation of the valence band (CMVB) design rules, originally formulated for Cu-based delafossite oxides. Four generalizations emerge: linear Cu coordination is not required, as tetrahedral coordination (CN = 4) is compatible with p-type TCM character; the mechanism extends to halide-based systems with I $5p$ anion states; the Cu $d$ state energy center $ε_d$ is a quantitative descriptor for valence band dispersion; and Cu undercoordination in monovalent-anion hosts drives intrinsic p-type carrier generation through stoichiometric charge balance. These results establish a generalized computational framework for the design of p-type halide TCMs.

infographic.key_insight: A high-throughput DFT search across CuI-based ternary compounds identified 58 candidate p-type transparent conductors, showing that p-type TCM design rules extend beyond delafossite oxides to halide systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study expands the materials design space for transparent electrodes in transparent electronics and tandem photovoltaics by providing a screened set of stable, optically transparent, low-hole-mass candidates.
method: Minima hopping method was used to explore CuI-based ternary X–Cu–I structures.
Density functional theory screened candidates for thermodynamic stability, optical transparency, and light hole effective mass.
The results were used to test and generalize chemical modulation of the valence band design rules.
infographic.evidence_signal: From the abstract, 58 candidates were identified, including 49 previously unreported materials and 20 degenerate semiconductors; Cu2FI2 is highlighted with a calculated gap of 3.75 eV and hole effective mass of 0.262 m0.
infographic.watch_item: The reported candidates come from computational screening, so experimental synthesis, defect control, and carrier transport validation are still needed before device use.
infographic.paper_title: High-throughput computational discovery of CuI-based ternary $p$-type transparent conductors
